new.front: Who compiled the Analects, and when?
new.back: Confucius's disciples, after his death

new.front: In the Analects, what do the “gentleman” and the “petty person” stand for?
new.back: The gentleman is always good — the model to follow; the petty person shows what not to do

new.front: Why is the Analects written in short, pithy sayings?
new.back: It spoke to an almost completely illiterate population, so it was passed on by memory — each idea distilled to its simplest form

new.front: According to the 10/01 lecture, how do most religions present themselves?
new.back: As universal and timeless

new.front: What did Confucius's ethics draw on?
new.back: Longstanding ideas of morality

new.front: Which three things make up goodness, for Confucius?
new.back: Xiao (filial piety), ren (benevolence) and li (ritual)

new.front: How are Confucian relationships ordered, and what does each side owe?
new.back: All but one — friend and friend — are hierarchical. The subordinate must be dutiful; the superior must care for them and be kind. In filial piety, the parents are the superiors.

new.front: Which practice is part of filial piety, and central to Confucianism?
new.back: Ancestor worship

new.front: What does the Analects allow a child to do when their parents are in the wrong, and what must follow?
new.back: Gently remonstrate with them. If they don't take it to heart, stay respectful, don't oppose them, and follow their lead diligently without resentment.

new.front: What does Confucius say to do if your parents commit a crime and insist on it?
new.back: Cover up for them — even by taking the blame yourself

new.front: How did filial piety apply to a married woman?
new.back: Her in-laws became like her parents, since a wife moved into her husband's house

new.meaning: benevolence — the desire to do good; very simply, care for others

new.text: Ren in the Analects: “Ren is {{c1::to love people}}”; “When in public, comport yourself as if {{c2::you were receiving an important guest}}”; “Do not impose upon others {{c3::what you yourself do not desire}}”

new.meaning: ritual — doing everything according to the proper rites

new.front: How far does li, Confucian ritual, reach?
new.back: From grand state ceremonies to the proper way to fasten one's lapel

new.front: Where do the rites of li come from, and what idea lies behind that?
new.back: From older societies, especially the Zhou dynasty — the idea that old things are good

new.text: Confucius's ethics held that society should be ruled by {{c1::a meritocracy of educated men}}; that all people have {{c2::the capacity for self-cultivation}}; and that society is {{c3::fundamentally unequal}}, bound by {{c4::reciprocal relationships}}
new.extra: In those relationships, superiors are to be benevolent and subordinates are to obey.

new.text: The case that Confucianism is not a religion: Confucius is {{c1::not a god or a divine force}}; you needn't {{c2::pray, go to a temple, or read a specific book}}; you needn't {{c3::worship anything or believe Confucius was a god}}; and you can {{c4::practise it as a philosophy}}
new.extra: From a western perspective this “no” is the most common answer.

new.front: What caveat weakens “Confucius is not a god” as a reason Confucianism isn't a religion?
new.back: In East Asia there is no strict line between natural and supernatural, as there is in the West

new.text: The case that Confucianism is a religion: after Confucius died, {{c1::more religious aspects were added}}; there are {{c2::temples to Confucius, with animal sacrifices and rituals}}; some people {{c3::pray to Confucius}}; and it {{c4::asks you to follow principles to achieve goodness}}, as a religion does

new.front: What did later temples to Confucius borrow from Buddhism?
new.back: Ideas such as statues

new.front: Who was Mengzi, and when did he live?
new.back: A Confucian philosopher of the 4th century BCE

new.front: What was Mengzi's relationship to Kongzi (Confucius)?
new.back: He never met him, but tried to practise and teach Kongzi's Way

new.front: How is Mengzi ranked in China?
new.back: Second only to Kongzi in importance

new.front: What is the Mengzi, and where does the name “Mencius” come from?
new.back: The collection of Mengzi's sayings; “Mencius” is the Jesuits' Latinisation

new.front: How is the Mengzi divided?
new.back: Into 7 books, each with an A and a B part, each divided again into short “chapters” — hence references like 2A6

new.front: Whose teachings did Mengzi treat as the intellectual opponents of the Way?
new.back: Yang Zhu's and Mozi's

new.front: What did Mozi advocate?
new.back: Universal consequentialism: judging every action only by its consequences for the benefit of all, with everyone's benefit counting equally — hence Mohist “impartial caring”

new.front: What does Yang Zhu seem to have taught, and how did Mengzi see him?
new.back: That excessive sacrifice for others goes against human nature. Mengzi saw him as egotistical.

new.front: Where did Mengzi agree with Yang Zhu, and where did he part ways?
new.back: He agreed that humans have a nature they should follow, but argued that it contains virtuous inclinations — so ethical cultivation is tending that nature

new.front: How did Mengzi think people can discover their moral inclinations?
new.back: Through thought experiments

new.front: What did Mengzi say destroys the goodness of human nature?
new.back: A bad environment, and failure to cultivate oneself — the nature is good, but people are not necessarily good

new.front: What did Mengzi see as a prerequisite for developing a good nature?
new.back: Basic needs, such as food, being met

new.front: What does advanced ethical cultivation require, for Mengzi?
new.back: A teacher

new.front: How did Mengzi disagree with the Mohists about love?
new.back: They said love for all should be equally great; he said love for family, kin and those closer must be greater

new.front: What did Mengzi say of basing one's actions on benefit or profit?
new.back: That it is self-defeating

new.front: In Mengzi's Book One, what does he tell a king who wants profit?
new.back: That he should seek benevolence and righteousness instead

new.front: What is Mengzi's point in the parable of the soldiers who ran fifty paces?
new.back: Those who ran fifty paces, laughing at those who ran a hundred, had fled the battle just the same — said to a king who thought he governed well

new.front: What did a king's pity for an ox being led to sacrifice show, according to Mengzi?
new.back: That he has compassion

new.front: Why did Mengzi compare that king to someone who can lift 500 lbs but not a feather?
new.back: He showed kindness to the ox but not to his people — not because he can't, but because he won't

new.front: What did Mengzi compare a king's wish to dominate by military force to?
new.back: Climbing a tree to find a fish

new.front: What would benevolent government bring a king, according to Mengzi?
new.back: Everyone would want to come to his markets, fields and roads

new.front: What does Mengzi call failing to give people a livelihood and then punishing them for crime?
new.back: Trapping them

new.text: A good livelihood, for Mengzi: “In good years, one is {{c1::always full}}. In years of famine, one {{c2::escapes death}}” — and one can {{c3::serve one's father and mother, and nurture one's wife and children}}

new.front: How did Mengzi answer a king who excused himself as fond of wealth, and then as fond of sex?
new.back: If the ruler lets the common folk have the same — wealth, and the same privileges — that is in line with the Way

new.text: Mengzi on the execution of King Zhou: one who violates benevolence is {{c1::a thief}}; one who violates righteousness is {{c2::a mutilator}}; such a person is {{c3::a mere fellow}} — “I have heard of the execution of the fellow Zhou, but not of the killing of one's ruler”
new.extra: The point: a ruler who doesn't act properly is no longer a legitimate ruler.

new.front: In Mengzi 2A6, what follows if a ruler extends people's natural feeling for others into how he governs?
new.back: He brings order to the whole world

new.text: Mengzi's four sprouts (2A6): compassion is the sprout of {{c1::benevolence}}; disdain is the sprout of {{c2::righteousness}}; deference is the sprout of {{c3::propriety}}; approval and disapproval is the sprout of {{c4::wisdom}}
new.extra: Your notes list three; the second, disdain (shame at wrongdoing), is from the text.

new.front: According to Mengzi 2A6, what follows if one “fills out” the four sprouts — and if one doesn't?
new.back: Filled out, they are enough to care for all within the four seas; neglected, one can't even serve one's parents

new.front: In Mengzi 6A1, what did Gaozi claim, and how did Mengzi answer?
new.back: Gaozi: human nature has to be moulded into righteousness, as willow is made into bowls. Mengzi: then people must be violated to be made good — which makes benevolence and righteousness a misfortune.

new.front: What is Gaozi's water analogy for human nature (Mengzi 6A2)?
new.back: Human nature is like water, which flows out of whatever opening it's given — so it is neutral, neither good nor bad

new.front: How did Mengzi turn Gaozi's water analogy around?
new.back: Water naturally flows downward. It can be dammed or splashed upward, but that goes against its nature — so human nature is good.

new.front: In Mengzi 6A4, what did Gaozi claim about benevolence and righteousness?
new.back: That benevolence is internal and righteousness external — Mengzi disagreed

new.front: In Mengzi 6A6, how did Mengzi answer Gaozi's claim that human nature is neither good nor bad?
new.back: All humans have the potential to be good

new.front: When did Xunzi live, relative to China's unification?
new.back: He was one of the last exponents of Confucian thought before unification in 221 BCE

new.front: In what form has Xunzi's thought come down?
new.back: Essays

new.front: How did Xunzi treat Confucianism's critics?
new.back: He defended Confucianism against them, but learned from them and took in their insights — Zhuangzi's above all, though their views differed a great deal

new.front: Which threat from within Confucianism did Xunzi see in Mengzi?
new.back: The idea that human nature is good, which he thought did away with the need for ritual to guide behaviour

new.front: What did Xunzi mean by saying human nature is bad?
new.back: Not that people delight in evil, but that they have no inborn guide to right conduct — so they need the external guide of ritual

new.front: Where does Xunzi agree with Mengzi about goodness, and where does he differ?
new.back: Everyone has the potential for it — but for Xunzi, reaching it is a very hard and arduous process

new.front: According to Xunzi (ch. 23), what are people born with?
new.back: A desire for profit, other desires, and feelings of hate and dislike — and following them is bad

new.front: Where does following human nature lead, for Xunzi?
new.back: To strife in society, and eventually violence

new.front: What does Xunzi say people need in order to reach righteousness?
new.back: The transforming influence of teachers and models, and the guidance of ritual and righteousness — ritual no one knows from birth

new.front: What is Xunzi's image of the crooked wood?
new.back: Crooked wood must await steaming and straightening on the shaping frame; only then does it become straight. Mengzi had objected that shaping people, like turning willow into bowls, violates their nature.

new.front: Why did the ancients establish ritual, according to Xunzi?
new.back: To be a good influence on the common people

new.front: How does Xunzi disagree with Mengzi about learning?
new.back: For Mengzi, learning brings out people's inherent good; for Xunzi, ritual and righteousness come from effort

new.front: How does Xunzi tell what comes from inborn nature?
new.back: Desires come from it: they respond to stimulation with no delay between perception and reaction. So whatever has a delay is not from innate nature.

new.front: Why does Xunzi say people's wish to be good shows their nature is bad?
new.back: People desire what they lack

new.front: What does Xunzi ask of Mengzi's view of ritual?
new.back: If human nature is good, why would ritual be needed at all? Mengzi would say ritual brings an already-good nature into line with Heaven.

new.front: What did Mengzi add to Confucianism about authority?
new.back: That you don't always have to follow it

new.front: How were Mengzi's ideas received?
new.back: They were hugely popular, and many of his statements became common sayings

new.front: What is Mengzi's well analogy meant to show?
new.back: Everyone has a heart sensitive to others' suffering: anyone who saw a baby about to fall into a well would be alarmed — not to impress the parents or win a good name

new.front: What does Mengzi say of someone who wouldn't be alarmed by the baby at the well?
new.back: That they are not a human being — the feeling is that fundamental

new.front: How did the ancient kings' compassion show itself, for Mengzi?
new.back: In compassionate policies

new.front: How do Mengzi's priorities among xiao, li and ren differ from Kongzi's?
new.back: Kongzi might put xiao and li above ren — not turning in one's parents. Mengzi weighs them differently: see his answer on the killing of King Zhou, and his hint to King Xuan of Qi that a bad government should be removed.

new.front: What did Xunzi say about the sacrifice for rain?
new.back: It has no special mechanism — performing it has no effect on the rain

new.front: If the rain sacrifice does nothing, why does Xunzi say we perform such rites?
new.back: To give things proper form — though common people take them as contact with spirits. Practised society-wide, they make individuals and society good.

new.front: Why does Xunzi's view of ritual move Confucianism further from being a “religion” in western eyes?
new.back: He denies the rites any supernatural effect: they exist for form and moral formation

new.front: What do Ban Zhao and Song Ruozhao discuss?
new.back: The Confucian role for women

new.front: Who founded Neo-Confucianism, and what was it?
new.back: Zhu Xi — a revival of Confucianism after a decline

new.front: What did Zhu Xi's Neo-Confucianism focus on?
new.back: The family as the foundational unit, and the practical application of moral principles
